title: Biestek v. Berryhill (2019)
summary: A vocational expert's refusal to produce the private survey data behind her job numbers does not categorically prevent her testimony from counting as substantial evidence; the inquiry is case by case.
notes:
Key line: "The inquiry, as is usually true in determining the substantiality of evidence, is case-by-case." (Kagan, J.)

Citation: 587 U.S. 97 (2019).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was Michael J. Biestek, a former carpenter and general laborer on construction sites who applied for Social Security disability benefits after developing degenerative disc disease, hepatitis C and depression. The respondent was Nancy A. Berryhill, Acting Commissioner of Social Security. The vocational expert whose testimony was at issue, Erin O'Callaghan, had served as an expert in agency proceedings for five years and had more than ten years of experience counseling people with disabilities about employment; she was a contractor with the agency and not a party. The Seventh Circuit, whose categorical rule Biestek asked the Court to adopt, was not involved in the case.
sections.Material Facts: Biestek claimed eligibility for benefits as of October 2009. At a hearing on July 21, 2015, the administrative law judge had to decide whether he could transition to less demanding work, which required identifying jobs he could perform and whether they existed in significant numbers in the national economy. O'Callaghan testified that a person with Biestek's limitations could work as a bench assembler or sorter and that 240,000 bench assembler jobs and 120,000 sorter jobs existed nationally. On cross examination she said the numbers came from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and her own labor market surveys. Biestek's lawyer asked her to produce the surveys; she declined because they were part of confidential client files. When counsel suggested redacting client names, the ALJ said he would not require production in any form. The ALJ granted benefits from May 2013, when Biestek turned fifty, but denied them for October 2009 to May 2013, relying on O'Callaghan's testimony.
sections.Procedural History: Biestek sought judicial review in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan under 42 U.S.C. section 405(g), which makes the agency's factual findings conclusive if supported by substantial evidence. He argued that the expert's testimony could not be substantial evidence because she had refused to produce her supporting data. The district court rejected the argument in 2017. The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed, 880 F.3d 778 (2018), declining to follow the Seventh Circuit's rule in McKinnie v. Barnhart, 368 F.3d 907 (2004), and observing that the rule had not been a popular export. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on December 4, 2018, and affirmed on April 1, 2019, by a vote of 6 to 3.
sections.Issue: Whether a vocational expert's testimony about the number of jobs available in the national economy can constitute substantial evidence supporting an administrative law judge's denial of disability benefits when the expert, upon the applicant's request, refuses to provide the private market survey data on which the testimony is based. Biestek framed the proposed rule as a substantive rule about the quality of evidence rather than a procedural disclosure requirement, and as one triggered only when the applicant demands the data.
sections.Holding: The Court held that a vocational expert's refusal to provide private market survey data upon the applicant's request does not categorically preclude her testimony from counting as substantial evidence. Substantial evidence is more than a mere scintilla and means such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion. In some cases a refusal to disclose data, together with other shortcomings, will keep testimony from meeting that standard, but in others it will not. The inquiry is case by case, takes account of all features of the expert's testimony and the rest of the record, and defers to the ALJ who saw the hearing. Because Biestek asked the Court only to adopt the categorical rule, the Sixth Circuit's judgment was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Kagan began from common ground: absent any demand, an expert's testimony may be substantial evidence even without supporting data, as with a well credentialed expert who explains her survey methodology, answers all questions and is contradicted by nothing in the record. The question was why one additional fact, a refusal of a request for the data, should make such testimony categorically inadequate. Biestek's arguments contained nuggets of truth but could not support a flat rule. A refusal may support an adverse inference that the expert is hiding something, but the inference is not always required; if the ALJ otherwise trusts the expert and thinks she has good reason to keep client data private, the refusal need not matter. A refusal may also impede cross examination, and courts may consider such obstacles, but an applicant can still probe the expert's sources and methods, and the absence of data limits cross examination equally whether or not a demand was made. Social Security hearings are informal and not bound by the rules of evidence, so the federal court rule requiring experts to produce their data does not apply. Sometimes withholding data will prevent testimony from being substantialwhere the expert has no good reason for secrecy and her testimony lacks other markers of reliability; sometimes it will not. The Court did not decide whether substantial evidence supported the denial in Biestek's own case, because he had not asked it to.

topics.lrs-n-substantial-evidence: Expert testimony based on undisclosed data receives contextual assessment rather than categorical exclusion.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 6 to 3. Justice Sotomayor dissented, agreeing with Justice Gorsuch that the expert's conclusory testimony in this case, offered without any description of her surveys and cut off from cross examination when the ALJ intervened, was not substantial evidence, and stressing the ALJ's duty in an inquisitorial proceeding to develop the record. Justice Gorsuch, joined by Justice Ginsburg, dissented, arguing that an expert's bottom line conclusion supported only by a claim of readily available evidence she refuses to produce is the kind of conclusory evidence courts have long held insubstantial, that the refusal warrants an adverse inference, and that the Court should have resolved the narrower category of cases like Biestek's rather than leaving lower courts in limbo.
